page.title: Behind the Build · Samantha Paras
page.meta: How QuestKeeper moves data three different ways (public rules, account-based characters, and enemy stats kept from players), explained without needing to read the code.
header.h1: How QuestKeeper keeps a DM's secrets secret
short.label: The short version (no code needed)
short.intro: QuestKeeper moves three kinds of information, and each one travels differently:
short.1: Rules and spells are public, so they come through my own server from a public source.
short.2: Characters are saved to your account. Joining a table also lets that table's DM read your character sheet.
short.3: Enemy stats are hidden even from the players at the table. So the rules that need them run in the database, and players get back only the result.

panel.1.heading: Public rules travel through my backend
panel.1.body: Your browser asks QuestKeeper's backend. The backend asks the public D&D 5e SRD API, then returns it. The backend returns each category in a consistent response wrapper. Keeping the outside API behind my own server gives me one place to add validation, caching and source information later, without touching the frontend.
panel.1.phoneNote: Keeping the outside API behind my own server gives me one place to add validation, caching and source information later.
panel.2.heading: Account data goes straight to Supabase
panel.2.body: Signing in, saving characters, uploading portraits and joining live tables all talk to Supabase directly. Row-level security decides who can access which rows. Your characters belong to your account. The table-sharing policy lets its DM read your character sheet; it does not grant editing access.
panel.2.phoneNote: Signing in, saving characters, uploading portraits and joining live tables all talk to Supabase directly. Row-level security decides who can access which rows.

panel.3.heading: The rule runs where the secret lives
panel.3.body: A player sends their roll. A database function looks up the enemy's armor class in a table restricted to the DM, checks the roll, and returns the result without including the AC. The function returns hit, miss, critical hit or waiting for the DM. A natural 1 misses and a natural 20 is critical; other rolls wait for the DM when no AC is set. Players see the enemy's name, the damage it has taken, and whether it's Healthy, Bloodied or Down. The migration definitions also leave the secrets table out of the Realtime publication used for table updates.
panel.3.tech: Example: rpc("attack_roll", { p_natural: 17, p_bonus: 5, … }) → "hit". The result depends on the target's AC and the function's other checks.
panel.3.phoneNote: A natural 1 misses and a natural 20 is critical; other rolls wait for the DM when no AC is set. The migration definitions also leave the secrets table out of the Realtime publication used for table updates.
panel.all.heading: Three data paths
panel.all.body: Public reference data, account-based character data with table-DM read access, and enemy details restricted to the DM. Pick a path to read about it.
why.h2: Why hiding it on screen wasn't enough
why.p: Anything a browser receives can be read in its developer tools. A "DM only" label on the screen wouldn't stop a curious player from opening the network tab. The fix had to change what gets sent, not just what gets shown.
checked.p: The project README records local checks of the database functions using DM, player and outsider identities. Those checks are not currently included as automated tests in the repository.
players.p: The DM sees the numbers. Players see a name, a status and the damage dealt.
